S065.name: Obsessions
S065.description: Recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges, or images that are experienced as intrusive and unwanted, and attempts to ignore or suppress them.

subtypes.Contamination Obsessions: Recurrent and intrusive worries about contamination, germs, or dirt.
subtypes.Pathological Doubt: Pathological doubt regarding safety or mistakes, such as whether doors are locked or gas valves are closed.
subtypes.Symmetry and Exactness Obsessions: A strong urge that items must be lined up exactly or be symmetrical.
subtypes.Forbidden or Taboo Thoughts: Intrusive thoughts involving aggressive (harming others), sexual, or religious content that are prohibited.
subtypes.Somatic Obsessions: Persistent and specific fear that one might have a serious disease.

S066.name: Compulsions
S066.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to an obsession or to prevent anxiety/distress; clearly excessive or not realistically connected.

subtypes.Cleaning or Washing Compulsions: Repetitive acts to remove contamination, such as hand washing, showering, or excessive cleaning.
subtypes.Checking Compulsions: Repeatedly checking items like door locks, gas stoves, or switches to prevent danger.
subtypes.Ordering and Arranging Compulsions: Organizing objects in a specific order or at a precise angle to reduce anxiety.
subtypes.Mental Acts: Mental rituals performed internally, such as praying, counting, or repeating specific words silently.
subtypes.Repeating Rituals: Repeating specific actions (e.g., standing up, passing through a door) a set number of times.

symptom.disease_info: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) is characterized by recurrent, intrusive thoughts, images, or urges (obsessions) and/or repetitive behaviors or mental acts (compulsions) that the person feels driven to perform. These symptoms are time-consuming or cause significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. The course is often chronic with waxing and waning severity, frequently exacerbated by stress, increased responsibility, or role transitions. OCD is distinguished from generalized anxiety and other disorders by the presence of specific, stereotyped obsessions and compulsions that are recognized as excessive or unreasonable at some point and are not solely attributable to psychotic processes or the direct effects of substances or medical conditions.

patient.stressor: Edward’s pattern of being highly structured and meticulous had long been seen as a strength, especially through graduate school and the early years of his mechanical engineering job. During a major product rollout last year, he was put in charge of coordinating multiple design teams, managing tight client deadlines, and ensuring compliance with new sustainability standards, all while studying for the PE exam in his off-hours. Around this period, he began spending increasingly long hours at his desk well after everyone else had left, rechecking design files and project plans in a way that started to interfere with his sleep, jogging routine, and social life with the paddleboarding club. The situation came to a head when he missed a key beach clean‑up event he had organized because he couldn’t pull himself away from repeatedly reviewing a relatively minor CAD change; his manager later gently pointed out that his productivity was paradoxically dropping, which prompted Edward to seek psychiatric help after recognizing that his own mental routines felt out of his control.
patient.chief_complaint: “I keep getting stuck redoing the same checks and routines over and over at work, even when I know they’re unnecessary, and it’s starting to derail my projects and my life.”
